title: Why Pieter Levels launched 12 startups in 12 months: finish and ship small
summary: Levels explains his 2014 challenge to launch one startup per month. He diagnoses creatives' two killers, not finishing and fear of launching, and argues for starting small, exposing yourself to market forces, and defining a startup as a new product that grows fast.

principles.text: Forcing yourself to ship on a fixed cadence beats perfectionism; finishing and launching are the real bottlenecks, not building.
principles.quote: I can already build stuff. My challenge is to actually finish and launch my projects. So for the next 12 months, I’ve set the goal to launch 12 startups in 12 months.

principles.text: Fear of failure makes builders under-launch or never launch because they compare reality to a fantasy launch.
principles.quote: The fear of failure takes over so we don’t put enough effort into launching or we don’t launch at all.

principles.text: Start small instead of waiting for a big vision; the big vision comes after market fit with an MVP.
principles.quote: The big vision happened after they found a market fit with their MVPs.

principles.text: Taking action beats idle planning; you learn by exposing yourself to the market, even if you do the wrong thing first.
principles.quote: You’ll figure out what you need to do by exposing yourself to the world (and its market forces). And especially if you’re not experienced like me, I think it’s better to start small first, and slowly build bigger things.

principles.text: A startup is a new product that grows fast; building is easy, growing is hard.
principles.quote: Delivering a new product is the easy part, growing it fast is the hard part.

principles.text: Time-box validation: if a product shows no demand within a month of launching the MVP, treat it as failed and move on.
principles.quote: My plan is to see if I can get market fit in one month, and if it doesn’t show any signs of being somewhat in demand, I consider it failed.
